title: The Dragon’s Pact
description: A desperate prince. An ancient dragon. A bargain that could save a kingdom—or cost him his soul.
paragraphs: Dragons once ruled the world. It was a saying as old as time, and it was a fact. Dragons were once considered the guardians of the realm, the literal pillars on which peace was built. Legend has it that when the Evil Gods banded together to spread chaos across the land, the Creator sent dragons to cleanse the realm and protect it from all threats. However, in the present day, these former guardians are seen as nothing more than living disasters.

Prince Thane of Starhaven grew up with an infatuation for tales of dragons. For every glorious epic of a dragon and a knight bound together by fate to protect the realm, there were hundreds more tales of dragons imprisoned or slain for the evil they had wrought. As Thane delved deeper into these stories, he struggled to distinguish fact from fiction. One undeniable truth remained: dragons existed, whether man wanted them to or not. Thane never understood the widespread hatred for dragons. He could grasp why there were entire corps dedicated to slaying wyverns—savage creatures born of chaos that only happened to resemble dragons.

To Thane, comparing wyverns to the dragons he admired was insulting. Wyverns were a horrid far cry from the majestic nature of true dragons. Thane's fascination with dragons bordered on worship; their majestic nature captivated him completely. This was a problematic trait, as few people still believed in the power of the dragons of old as Thane did. Thanks to the dark practices of past dragon worshippers, the realm viewed such devotion with disdain. Thane was fortunate to have been born in Starhaven, where his parents, King Roland and Queen Aera Asterisk, were supportive of his interest in dragons. Had he been born anywhere else, his fascination might have been met with severe disapproval.

Thane's love for dragons began with the bedtime stories his parents shared, tales they had grown up with themselves. According to these stories, Starhaven was once home to a dragon known as "The Star." While most dragons were considered elemental, The Star earned its name by attaining a power closer to that of the gods: the power of fate. Legend has it that during the Dark Ages, a prince in dire need of protection for his realm sought out this dragon and made a pact with it. In return, he was given the sword known as "Star Crosser," the legendary blade that now marks Starhaven's banners. When peace finally reigned, the prince offered his realm as The Star’s new abode, thus giving birth to the name Starhaven.
This legacy shaped Thane’s worldview.

Thane knew the legend of 'The Prince and the Star' could have been nothing more than a fairy tale, but when the Paling Plague struck Starhaven and left thousands dead, he took a small band of his most loyal men and set out at once to find the lair of this legendary dragon, hoping it might be willing to form a new contract with him. He sought to save not just his realm, but the lives of his parents as well.

On the fourth day of his quest, Thane and his men set up camp on the edge of a region no sane man would dare to trespass. It was a no man's land, unnamed and forsaken, crawling with monsters and wyverns. Based on all the texts and accounts he had studied, Thane figured that not only was it the least explored region within his territory, it was also believed to house a great evil. Thane was convinced that if there was any place for a dragon to remain undisturbed, it had to be here.

That night, he perched at the desk within his tent, staring at the letters his younger brother had sent him. Prince Arden Asterisk was three years younger than Thane, and although they never saw eye to eye, Thane could tell that his brother was finally losing his patience. For the past decade, while Thane absorbed himself in ancient texts and tomes regarding his infatuation with the winged guardians of old, Arden had made a name for himself on and off the battlefield. Not only had he defended their kingdom from monsters and marauders, but he had also graduated from one of the finest knight academies within the kingdom.

Although their parents never favored one over the other, there had always been competition between them. Thane excelled at the sword and showed an affinity for magic, though he was too much of a pacifist, buried in his books, to put any of his talents to good use. Despite Arden's many achievements, he always felt the need to do more.

The brothers still loved each other dearly, but a year ago, when the Paling Plague struck their land and their father fell gravely ill, their views created a great divide between them. Arden had become a regent, sitting at the council table to fill their father's post because Thane preferred to head out into the region to "investigate." No one believed Thane was actually up to any good. In their eyes, the prince was an aloof dragon lover who had been spoiled all his life— but that was far from the truth.

In pursuit of his hobbies, Thane had read much more than just fairy tales and history books. He had also versed himself in alchemy, magic, and just enough science to understand that the Paling Plague that ravaged their land was beyond the reach of common spells and potions. Arden, however, would never listen when Thane tried to explain this fact to him. Arden was formally educated and praised among his peers; how could he believe that his self-taught brother knew better than him and all the mages and alchemists serving their father's court?

“Are you awake, Prince Thane?” A soft voice snapped him from his musings as he turned his eyes away from the letter to permit his visitor into his tent. He wasn’t surprised when the doe-eyed ‘Scale’ Alana Thorne sheepishly strolled in. Alana was a young mage with a history shrouded in mystery. She had hair as white as snow, flawless white skin, and was a beauty to behold, but no one wanted to be associated with her because she was a ‘Scale.’

Curse or mutation, no one could truly tell the origin of the Scales. They were a people shunned for bearing draconian eyes and often having skin marked by dark scales. Thane’s reputation was already in shambles, and the fact that he’d taken Alana off the streets because he believed she was talented in magic did not do him any favors.
“What is it, Alana?” he asked. “Did you have another premonition?”

Her lips curled up in a distasteful way that ruined her pretty face. Five years ago, when Alana was only fifteen, she had seen Thane pick her off the streets. Before that fateful morning, she had lain on the side of the road, dying of starvation, only to wake up bathed and clothed by maids within the castle under orders from the young Prince Thane. He had picked her up himself while returning from a private trip beyond the castle walls.

She never realized she even had an affinity for magic until she approached one of the castle mages to take her as an apprentice so she could serve Thane better for his kindness. Shortly after she became his personal Aide and in the years that followed, she earned his trust, and he earned hers. Eventually, she confided in him about her gift of premonition. She had no control over them, but she was well aware of what they were. When she had a premonition of the Paling Plague and a dragon being connected, she never expected that Thane would cast all his duties aside and take it upon himself to find the dragon 'Star' from the legends to save his people. She felt guilty for making them come this far away from home on nothing more than a hunch.
‘If Star was real, then someone else would have found it centuries ago,’ she frowned to herself as Thane sighed at her mute display.

“You’re making that face again.” Thane crossed his arms. He disliked when she got like this, he always knew that whatever was coming to roll of her tongue was either going to be depressingly pessimistic or nagging. “How are the knights faring?”

“Tired… and wary. They think the prince’s pet ‘Scale’ is leading them all to an early grave,” Alana grumbled. Sir Galen and his men were loyalists to the royal family and would have gladly followed any of them into the jaws of death itself if it was demanded of them, so Thane could tell they hadn’t said such things— but that didn’t help Alana from doubting herself.

“Well… we’re here, and by this time tomorrow they’ll have smiles on their faces knowing you led us right to Star.” He smiled reassuringly, like he truly believed his own words. His optimism was like the sun; it smothered her gloomy side every time she tried to dissuade him. Honestly, she almost felt tempted to punch him, to give him some reason to see her the way everyone else did.
“What makes you so sure we’ll find it?” Alana’s eyes trailed to the letter bearing the Asterisk crest before Thane could hide it within his coat pocket. Her scowl deepened. “Your brother…”

“Will be glad we find the dragon and cure everyone when we’ve returned,” Thane responded defensively interrupting her midsentence as he got up and walked over. Alana’s eyes bore down on his sturdy frame. He was handsome in every sense of the word, with his muscles careful hidden with his robe, and the way his short dark hair framed his face. She owed him her life. He was her light, and she admired him. She knew that he was just as troubled as she was behind his boyish smile as his radiant lime-green eyes dawned on her. “You worry too much.”
“Sometimes I fear you don’t worry enough.” Alana broke away from his gaze defiantly as she turned to leave. “On the off chance we do find the Star… we don’t know if it’ll even choose to help us?”

Thane’s smile wavered for a moment as she excused herself, knowingly expecting that he’d respond with something annoyingly optimistic. Though she hadn’t noticed that even in her absence, Thane stood there feeling rather dazed. It wasn’t that he hadn’t considered the possibility of her words being true; he just wanted things to go their way so badly he was willing to ignore it.

As optimistic as Thane was, he wasn’t a fool. He knew that as majestic as dragons were, some of them were also capable of great malevolence. He was glad his men had escorted him this far, but he never intended to risk their lives on the gamble that the Star would be so kind as to help them. He waited until he was certain Alana had fallen asleep in her tent and the campfire had died down. Then, he discarded his robe to reveal the tunic and light armor he wore underneath. Escaping from his own camp was no problem; his men were competent, but he knew them well enough to memorize their routines and identify the easiest way to get by them.

When Thane made it to the forest, he steeled his resolve. He would find the Star and return before dawn. As impossible as it sounded, he’d picked a trick or too from the dragon slayer’s handbook and was certain he could pull it off with his skills. Suddenly, a mighty voice rang in his ears.
‘I must admit, you're a peculiar one…’

He felt his very being tremble as his vision of reality blurred into a myriad of colors before a new scene played out before him. He was in a lair lit by molten gold and lava coursing through the earth around a makeshift bed of bones and treasure. Atop it was the source of the voice, a giant dragon with sleek crimson scales that parted along its chest where golden scales formed a patch like that of a star. Thane gawked at his surroundings in terrified awe. 'Illusion?' he panicked, but all of it felt too real— the scents, the heat, and the dragon's curiously menacing gaze on his body. ‘No… was I teleported?’ Regardless of what it was, He instinctively fell to his knees.
The Prince had hoped to find the Star, but it had found him instead.

"I expected you and your men to march into my flames, yet you intrigued me by sparing them a dreadful fate and coming here yourself. I could have easily allowed you to wander those woods until the monsters finally overwhelmed you, but now I'm curious to know what drives you."

Thane, his voice trembling, explained how a plague was ravaging his land and that he needed the dragon's help to save his people. The dragon grunted, sounding rather disappointed as it refused, saying it was no healer. Thane was dazed but refused to back down.
"Aren't you the Star from the legends? Don't you command fate? I'm begging you, save my people."

"Do I look like a common Fae, granting wishes on a whim? ‘Star’... is that what your people call me now?" The dragon laughed, then flames bellowed from its mouth and unto Thane's body, engulfing him in a violent, searing pain as it relished in the prince’s suffering. "I am a power beyond your understanding. If you've come all this way to die, so be it."

The pain of burning was excruciating. Thane forced himself to his feet, every movement a struggle against the agony that consumed him. His skin felt like it was melting, his flesh searing, but he clenched his jaw and pushed through it.
"No... I didn't come here to die. I came here for my people. And I don't care how powerful or malevolent you are. I am Prince Thane of Starhaven, and I will save my people."

The dragon paused, laughing as it leaned closer. The fire vanished, and so did his wounds. Thane stared at the creature in terrified awe, knowing firsthand how easily it could erase him from existence.
"Even if it costs you your soul?" It smirked.

Thane hesitated. Had Alana been there, she would have stopped him, but Thane understood that what he was asking for was no mere favor. He had already made up his mind to do all within his power, and so he nodded. "Yes... even if it costs me my soul."
The dragon laughed as it dug one of its claws into Thane's chest. Thane roared in pain. The claw felt like a tree trunk being forced through his body as the world spun around him.
"So be it, Prince. You and I are now bound in the truest of pacts—my power for your soul..."
Thane could feel the dragon's pact taking hold of him, and he knew that when it spoke of taking his soul, it meant it. But if it meant Starhaven could be saved, he was willing to take it all.

title: A Thief’s Gambit
description: The kingdom’s greatest thief meets a vault that was never meant to keep him out.
paragraphs: The vault was a marvel of engineering, one that the kingdom of Nue had long boasted about with pride. Crafted by the finest artisans, it had become the stuff of legends, whispered about in taverns, detailed in books, and speculated over by treasure hunters and thieves alike. They said it was impenetrable, that no thief alive had a chance of making it through its myriad of traps and enchantments. It was said to be the finest piece of mechanical artistry in all the lands, designed to protect the kingdom's treasures for centuries to come.

Raul, however, was not convinced. He had heard similar stories before, and he knew well enough that rumors were often blown out of proportion. No vault was truly impenetrable. To him, this was merely another job, albeit one with a bit more notoriety than most. If anything, the exaggerated stories made it easier for him to focus. While others shied away from such a daunting task, Raul smirked at the challenge, knowing that he had the skill, the cunning, and the patience to succeed where others were too chicken shit to try.

As always he used the cover of night to his advantage, rappelling unto the fortress and snaking his way inside. His descent onto the platform (that led to the fortress’ vault) was as smooth as silk, the ropes he used nearly invisible against the night sky. The platform was tucked away from sight, accessible only to those who knew the layout of the kingdom’s fortifications. Raul had spent months preparing for this moment, memorizing guard rotations, analyzing patrol routes, and studying blueprints he had acquired through less-than-legal means. ‘The Thieving Shadow’ people called him, and for good reason. When Raul was determined they’d only ever caught a glimpse of him in the corner of their eyes, like a shadow, and the very next second he’d robbed them blind. Though today he had no intention of being seen in the slightest, he needed to be more than a shadow.

As he landed, his boots barely made a sound on the stone. The platform opened up to the vault entrance, and to Raul’s surprise, there were hardly any guards. Three, to be exact, standing like statues in the darkened hall. He had watched them long enough to know they were as armed to the teeth as they were incompetent. He imagined that they were stationed there to be nothing more than intimidating— maybe cut down any poor amateurs that were foolish enough to be caught. But when it came to him, it was as good as the vault being unguarded. These three weren’t the most alert soldiers— likely convinced that no one would be foolish enough to try and break into such a heavily reputed vault. They had no idea they were about to face one of the best thieves in Nue, no, the world.

Raul had little trouble getting past them. A few deft movements, and the guards were unconscious before they even realized what was happening. Their slumber was the only sound in the air as Raul turned his attention to the vault door. He half expected some intricate puzzle, maybe a magical lock, or even enchanted wards to keep intruders at bay. But what he found perplexed him.

The vault’s door was not what he imagined. Instead of glowing runes or pulsating magic, he was faced with a series of gears, large and small, interlocking and spinning slowly within the wall. The design was elegant, yes, but simple in a way that seemed at odds with all the rumors he had heard. Raul furrowed his brow, his eyes tracing the lines of the mechanism. It seemed to be a complex gear-based locking system, but where were the traps? Where were the layers of magical defenses?

Raul had come prepared with all manner of charms and silver, ready to face the enchantments he’d been told about. He carried amulets to ward off magical detection and had spent a small fortune on a cloak that supposedly repelled most scrying spells. But as he stood there, examining the vault door, he felt almost over-prepared.

‘What manner of treachery is this?’ He shrugged to himself, slipping his tools from his belt. He wasn’t one to complain about easy pickings. If the vault was simpler than anticipated, so be it. After all, this wasn’t about proving a point— it was about getting rich.

Raul knelt by the mechanism, his skilled fingers beginning to work through the gears. He could feel the resistance at first, the lock tight and intricate, but as he manipulated the gears, it became clear to him how it worked. One by one, the pieces slid into place. The satisfying click of metal against metal echoed through the corridor as the safe whirred and grinded to life.

The doors began to open, revealing the treasures inside. Raul couldn't help but whistle. Gold, jewels, and artifacts of incalculable value shimmered in the faint light. He allowed himself a brief moment of satisfaction. For all the talk, for all the warnings, this had been far easier than expected. With a smirk, he stepped inside the vault, his eyes gleaming as they swept over the bounty before him.

But then something shifted. A shiver ran down his spine, a faint sensation in the back of his mind— the kind that had kept him alive all these years. His sixth sense kicked in, a feeling of wrongness that he couldn’t quite shake. This was too easy.

He barely had time to react. A mist began to rise from the floor, swirling around his feet before he could make a move to escape. The world tilted around him, his limbs growing heavy as if they were encased in lead. His vision blurred, the treasures before him becoming distant and hazy. He tried to fight it, to resist the pull of unconsciousness, but it was too late. The last thing he remembered before collapsing was the soft sound of laughter echoing in the back of his mind.

Raul awoke in a darkened chamber, his body aching, his head pounding. He was bound to a chair, thick ropes securing his wrists and ankles. His mouth was dry, and his vision swam as he tried to focus. The room was dimly lit, and as his eyes adjusted, he saw figures standing before him, their faces obscured by shadows.
“Well, well,” came a voice from the shadows, deep and amused. “The infamous Raul. You’ve caused quite a stir.”

Raul’s mind raced as he took in his surroundings. He was alive, that much was clear. But why? The kingdom of Nue wasn’t known for mercy toward thieves. He had expected to wake up in a dungeon, if at all. Instead, he found himself in what appeared to be an interrogation room.
“What can I say?” Raul smirked despite the pounding in his head. “If that vault was your idea of a job interview, you should’ve just sent me a dove.”

The voice chuckled, stepping forward into the light. The man was tall, dressed in finely tailored robes, his face marked with the telltale signs of age and authority. “Would you have been inclined to accept, had we done so?”
“Probably not,” Raul admitted, his smirk widening. “But at least I wouldn’t have gotten knocked out by some fancy mist.”

The man laughed again, but this time there was a hardness to it. “You’re quite skilled, Raul. No one has gotten as far as you did. The vault was designed to test, not only to protect. And you passed with flying colors.”
Raul raised an eyebrow. “Is this the part where you praise me for my talents before locking me up?”
“No.” The man’s voice was calm but firm. “This is the part where we offer you a choice.”
Raul’s grin faltered slightly. “What kind of choice?”

“You’ve committed many crimes in this kingdom,” the man began, pacing slowly. “Theft, breaking into royal properties, forging documents… the list goes on. But we’re not here to punish you. We’re here to recruit you.”
Raul blinked. “Recruit me? For what?”
“There’s something we need stolen. Something that requires… a unique set of skills. Skills that you possess.”
Raul’s mind raced, his instincts telling him this was bad. Very bad. “And if I refuse?”

The man smiled, but it didn’t reach his eyes. “Let’s just say your future won’t be as bright. We have the power to ensure you never see daylight again, Raul. But we’d rather put your talents to good use.”
Raul forced a wry grin. “So what is it you want stolen?”

“All in good time,” the man said. “For now, consider yourself our guest. You’ll be given the tools you need, transportation, and of course… an incentive. You pull this job off, and you walk free. You fail…” He left the rest unsaid.
Raul sighed, leaning back in his chair. “Well, they don’t call me the master thief for nothing. I’ll hear you out.”
The man smiled again, and Raul knew he didn’t have a choice.
Blurb:

Raul, a master thief renowned for his daring exploits in the city of Nue, has built a reputation on outwitting guards, cracking impenetrable vaults, and disappearing without a trace. But when he's approached with the heist of a lifetime— to break into the kingdom's most prestigious vault. However, things quickly go awry and he finds himself caught in the heart of the vault, surrounded by a magic unlike any he's ever seen. When he wakes up, bound and imprisoned, he realizes that escaping the vault was never the point.

Instead of being sentenced for his crime, Raul is offered an unexpected proposition by the kingdom's secretive council: work for them, or spend the rest of his life rotting in a dungeon. The task? Steal a mysterious artifact from the neighboring nation of Tios, a rival kingdom locked in a delicate political balance with Nue. The stakes are higher than any job Raul has ever taken on before. But can even the greatest thief in the kingdom outwit forces that defy time, magic, and destiny itself?

title: The Lost Kingdom
description: An archaeologist searches for a lost civilization. Then she wakes up inside it.
paragraphs: The air was thick with dust as Marinette, a renowned archaeologist, and her team of eager but increasingly tired excavators, worked through the last layer of sand that concealed the entrance to the lost ruins of a civilization known only in myth: The Kingdom of Theros.

“Be careful!” Marinette called out as her team loosened a stone slab, carefully lowering it to the ground. The excavation had taken weeks of tireless work under the desert sun, and now they were close— closer than anyone had been in centuries. “We’ve come too far to rush this now.”

As the stone settled, the faint carving of Therosi runes became visible on the walls that framed the entrance. Marinette’s heart raced. No one had seen these symbols in thousands of years. Until recently, Theros had been nothing more than legend, a kingdom that flourished during the ancient world, far ahead of its time, before vanishing mysteriously. Scholars had argued over its existence, but today would mark its undeniable rediscovery.
Among the team, a younger archaeologist named Jared let out an audible sigh. He wiped the sweat from his brow and leaned on his shovel with a look of disinterest.
“Not feeling the excitement, Jared?” Marinette asked, her sharp eyes catching his expression.

“I just don’t get it,” he admitted with a shrug. “I mean, sure, we’re digging up an ancient civilization, but it’s just another kingdom, right? Aren’t they all the same? What’s so special about this one?”
Marinette stopped her work, brushing the dirt off her hands as she approached him. She wasn’t angry, but she knew this was a moment to teach him what he was about to be a part of.

“Let me tell you something, Jared,” she began, her voice soft but filled with wonder. “Theros wasn’t just another kingdom. It was a beacon of progress and innovation during its time. Long before other civilizations had mastered basic metallurgy, Theros was developing complex architectural designs, engineering marvels that we still can’t fully comprehend. Their philosophers were centuries ahead, discussing concepts of time, reality, and energy that modern science is only beginning to understand.”
Jared’s disinterest faltered as he listened, and the others gathered closer, intrigued by the story.

“They were masters of harnessing natural energies,” Marinette continued. “Not in the crude way we think of today, with electricity or steam, but in ways we can’t fully imagine. They built cities that shimmered with power, creating a utopia of sorts—a kingdom that some say was gifted by the gods. And then…” Her voice trailed off.
“What happened?” Jared asked, now leaning in.

“No one knows,” Marinette said gravely. “One day, Therosi artifacts disappeared from the historical record. No more writings. No more ruins. It’s like the entire kingdom vanished, swallowed by time. Until recently, most believed it was only a legend. But we… we might be the first people to lay eyes on these ruins in thousands of years.”
The team stood in silent awe, absorbing the weight of Marinette’s words. They weren’t just excavating another ruin. They were uncovering a lost part of human history.
“Now,” Marinette said, smiling at the newfound energy in their faces, “shall we continue?”

Motivated by their leader’s words, the team pressed on, carefully navigating through the narrow, stone-carved corridors. Their flashlights flickered against ancient murals of gods and beasts, of people who lived in a society far removed from their own. Every corner revealed new pieces of the past, each more mysterious than the last.
It wasn’t long before one of the team members, a woman named Nadia, called out excitedly. “Dr. Marinette! Over here! I think I found something!”

Marinette rushed over, her heart pounding with the thrill of discovery as the rest of the team gathered around Nadia, who was brushing dust away from a large, ornate tome. The cover was made of a strange, shimmering material, unlike anything they had encountered before. It seemed to pulse faintly in the dim light of the chamber.

Carefully, Marinette knelt and examined the symbols etched into the tome. Her fingers traced the ancient script as she began to translate aloud. “This… it speaks of power, of energy that flows through all things. ‘The Binding Source,’ it calls it. It claims the key to the kingdom’s strength lay within this energy.”

The moment she finished reading, a deep rumble echoed through the chamber. The ground beneath their feet trembled, and before anyone could react, a surge of bright energy exploded from the tome, sending them all crashing backward.

Marinette was flung against the stone wall, her vision going white from the impact. Her ears rang, and through the haze, she could barely make out the shouts of her team. The once-silent ruins were now alive with chaos—crumbling stone, falling debris, and the desperate cries of her colleagues.

She struggled to sit up, her head pounding. Colin and Nadia were helping one of their teammates, who had been knocked unconscious by the blast. “What the hell just happened?” Colin yelled over the deafening noise as he supported their injured friend.

Marinette tried to speak, but her voice felt distant, her mind struggling to make sense of what she had just seen. “It… it could’ve been some kind of natural gas explosion,” she stammered, though even as she said it, she knew it wasn’t true. The energy, the way it surged—there was nothing natural about it.
They needed to get out.

The team scrambled to their feet, rushing toward the exit as the temple continued to collapse around them. Marinette stumbled, her legs unsteady, but she pushed forward, the adrenaline keeping her upright.

But just as they neared the entrance, the floor beneath Marinette gave way. She barely had time to scream before she plunged into the darkness below, the world around her spinning into a blur. She was falling—falling through what felt like an endless chasm.

As she tumbled, strange, vivid colors danced before her eyes. They swirled and shifted, forming patterns and shapes that seemed both familiar and alien. Her mind couldn’t comprehend what she was seeing—visions of places she had never been, people she had never known. It was as if she were falling through time itself.
Then, just as abruptly as it had begun, the fall ended. She hit the ground hard, her body slamming into something soft but firm, and her vision went black.

Marinette couldn’t tell how long she was unconscious for. All she knew was that when she awoke, her body was sore, yet all her wounds had been treated. Her head throbbed, and as she blinked the haze from her eyes, she found herself lying in a small, dimly lit room. The walls were made of smooth stone, but they were unlike the ruins she had been excavating. They were clean, intact, as though untouched by the ravages of time.

Marinette groaned, pushing herself up on shaky arms. Her throat was dry, and her head spun, but she was alive. And someone had tended to her wounds. As her senses returned, she noticed movement from the corner of the room. A small figure was peeking at her from behind a pillar.
It was a child.

The child’s attire was strange, unlike anything Marinette had ever seen. They wore a tunic made from an unfamiliar fabric that shimmered faintly, almost like the material of the tome they had found. Their hair was adorned with intricate braids, and their skin had a faint glow to it, as though touched by the same energy that had surged through the ruins.
Marinette swallowed, her voice hoarse. “Hey… it’s okay. I’m not going to hurt you.”
But the moment she spoke, the child darted away, disappearing through an arched doorway. Groaning, Marinette forced herself to stand. Her legs were weak, but she had to find out where she was.

She followed the path the child had taken, her hand brushing against the smooth stone walls for support. The corridor was narrow but led her to an open space—a balcony. And when she stepped out onto it, her breath caught in her throat.

Below her stretched a vast city, gleaming with life. Towering spires rose toward the sky, their surfaces reflecting the light of a sun that Marinette couldn’t see. The buildings were intricately designed, their architecture like nothing she had ever encountered. Waterways flowed between the structures, feeding into a central fountain that shimmered with the same pulsing energy she had felt in the ruins.
The city was beautiful—breathtaking in its complexity and elegance. And yet, there was an otherworldly quality to it, as though it didn’t quite belong in the world she knew.
Marinette’s heart raced as the realization dawned on her.
She wasn’t just looking at the ruins of Theros
Somehow, impossibly, she was standing in the kingdom itself. A kingdom lost to time, now revealed before her eyes in all its ancient glory.
“By the stars…” she whispered, her voice trembling. “This is Theros”
Blurb:

Marinette, a renowned archaeologist, leads her team on an excavation of an ancient, forgotten civilization lost to time. But when a strange energy bursts from a discovered tome, the ruins collapse, and Marinette is plunged into an underground cavern. She wakes to find herself in a forgotten world, filled with impossible landscapes and structures, realizing that she has somehow been transported back in time to the civilization she once thought lost. With only her knowledge and wit to rely on, Marinette must unravel the mysteries of this vanished kingdom while navigating its cryptic inhabitants, hoping to find a way back to her own time.

title: Murder Mystery
description: A small-town café, a warm cup of tea, and a guest who will never make it home.
paragraphs: The jingle of the bell as another couple of satisfied customers shuffled out into the evening, put a smile on my face. I stepped out right after with a fond smile on my face. Judging from how much they loved my pastries I had no doubt that they’d be back again in the morning, ‘The tourists always love the scones.’ Uncle Lewis would chuckle if he’d been there to see them off. As the cold Autumn breeze graced me with its chill, I rubbed my hands together and shoved them in my apron. It didn’t do much to fight the chill, but it gave me a bit of relief.

It was the second week of November and the winter breeze was already upon us. I took a moment to myself and just glanced up at the sign of our little coffee shack. Up until yesterday it used to be named ‘Saveur Sucree.’— It was French for Sweet Flavour. With my Uncle’s passing, Lacie Hawkins and I decided there was no better time for a rebranding.

Today Pike Falls welcomed the new and improved 'Cafe Robusta’ to the neighbourhood. Lacie and I practically grew up together, but had it not been for me then maybe our little shack would have ended up with an odd name like ‘Cutie Pie’ or ‘Mochila’— but after days of ceaseless debating, Cafe Robusta was I final verdict, and the townsfolk seemed to love it. Lacie was an arts major and usually helped planned the events around town, she did a wonderful job with the shop’s new sign, now the old shack welcomed everyone who chanced upon it with an eye-catching flurry of soothing neon lights about its name and the cute signature of a cat, her personal touch.

I on the other hand, decided to make the most of the shop’s interior. Cafe Robusta used to be a tavern and was just as old as Pike Falls itself. Every inch of it was so rich in history, and I decoded to treasure that... just the way Lewis would have wanted me to.

Pike Falls’ a modest town, a few hours drive away from New York. Despite its mundane appeal most of the year, it was the type of place that bustled with life during this time of the year. Thanks to Halloween and the Apple picking games from last month, a lot of wine enthusiasts and tourists had come into time in anticipation for Pike Falls’ annual Cider contest.

There were a ton of events planned and I could already see a lot of new faces, exploring the streets with excited glints in their eyes. It was good for business. I loved the ever so cheerful aura to Pike Falls, I’d grown up here and it was moments like these that reminded me why I chose to stay. There were a few more minutes to closing, and I was already on the verge of turning the sign over and heading in to call it a day, when a soft voice called to me.

“Excuse me...” A lovely young lady greeted me. She seemed a bit over dressed in her thick dull grey coat, but with the chill in the air I couldn’t blame her, and she seemed flustered like she’d ran a short distance to get there. She held up a flyer and I smiled. It was the invite to the shop’s renaming, it was more than apparent to me that she must have come for Lacie and I's slice of heaven on earth. “I hope am not too late.”
“Of course not,” I beamed a smile at her as I helped her with the door. “We should still have a few scones, would you like tea or coffee?”
“That sounds nice.” She replied shyly as she took of her coat in front of me, “I prefer tea please.”

“Coming right up.” I grinned as I stepped in after her. The warmth wafting through the shop from the fire Lacie had got going in the fireplace was a blessing from the cold and from the sigh of relief our guest let out, I could tell that she liked it too. I ushered the lady to a table not too far from the door and briskly whipped her a full cream tea and some scones.
“They look delicious. How much will this be?” She asked as she reached for her wallet. Her lips pursed as her wide Hazel brown eyes stared up at me.

“Its on the house.” I waved as I saw a genuine look of glee wash over her face as she thanked me. It was look I loved to get from all my customers, their satisfaction was just as satisfying as knowing Lacie and I had already met our quota for the month, and were practically running our shop for the joy of it.

I had been too distracted by work to realise just how exhausting it all was. I stepped into the kitchen and took my apron off. I’d given the lady the last of our scones and figured I’d settle for some tea myself when a familiar whistle caught my attention. It was Lacie, she was in our favourite spot by the fireplace and when I turned to face her, she held up a tray full of the left over scones.

It was thoughtful of her, I mused when I walked over and she patted the chair beside her. There was a mug of hot chocolate waiting for me and she had a catty look on her face when I joined her. “How thoughtful of you...” I grinned as I took my seat as lifted the mug to my lips. The smell was alluring with a faint milky scent to it, Lacie watched me closely. I could tell she was expecting a compliment and after my first sip, compliments were all I had.

“You like?” She beamed at me. Usually, she made my chocolate either too milky or she’d  put in way too much sugar, but today it was just the way I liked it. Just sweet enough for me to taste every little bit of it.
“Yes...” I admitted through pursed lips, “Its okay for once.”
Lacie took a scone from the tray, but wouldn’t let herself finish chowing down on it before she started talking. “So, guess who got a job at the Cider fair this week.”

I didn’t like when Lacie was unladylike—which was way more often than I would like to admit— but the serenity about the shop was enough that I could tolerate it a lot better this time. The answer to her question was obvious, and I was happy for her. “Are they actually going to pay this time?” I asked,

Lacie and I worked with a quota in mind. At the start of every month we planned to make enough to cover our monthly expenses and spill over for repairs and emergencies, thanks to all the tourist we had enough to go by for the next few months, but I wasn’t fond of when the town committee talks Lacie into doing jobs for free, merely because she’s from her. Lacie might love to do so but to me it feels as though she’s being taken advantage of.
She grinned.

Lacie went on and on about how she’d taken my advice and stood her ground about getting paid for her services, and it impressed me that the ever so rigid Committee had agreed, but that wasn’t all. “Justin is going to be working on the booths with me.”

My eyes lit up. Justin Mansfield was a handsome bachelor that lived across the block from our street. We all went to the same high-school and hearing his name was a trip down memory lane. “Justin is back in town?— since when?”

“I was just as surprised as you are.” Lacie squealed with a blush in her cheeks. ‘How many years had it been? 8? Or was it 10?’ I paused as I watched Lacie intently. From the looks of it, she still had a crush on him. Back in the day she was head over hills for Justin but just never had the courage to tell him. Now, she was a lovely grown woman, with the charms and the wiles of one.

This was looking up to be very eventful week. Suddenly, a loud thud accompanied by the sound of crashing ceramic startled me. ‘The kitchen!’ I thought instinctively as I shot out of my chair, ‘No... it couldn’t be.’ There was no one in the kitchen, and the sound came from the opposite direction. I glanced over to the table where the young lady I’d let in was having her tea, but she wasn’t in her chair— she was laying motionless on the floor instead.
“Lacie!” I called as I rushed over to the lady, “Call for help,”

Lacie looked confused and searched for her phone while I got on my knees beside the lady to help her up. “Are you okay?” I bellowed as I held her hand... it was cold to the touch. I let her hand fall limp to the floor as I became petrified by fear. She was pale as a ghost, I'd seen this before.
The lady was dead.

title: Romance
description: She has a future to build. He has an invitation she has no intention of accepting.
paragraphs: It was a lovely evening, no better night for a party than on the day of the lord. The music that accompanied the clattered of glasses and laughter as all the guests danced and enjoyed their evening would seem as though the entirety of its scenery was birth for her and her alone. Chastity was a beauty to behold, in her long, elegant evening dress of deep green satin, as she whirled around the dance floor with one man after another, thoroughly enjoying the swishing sound the dress made, the way it contrasted with her flaming hair as the lamination from the curious moon in the sky and the lights from the hall settled on her. She was the official hostess of this dinner party. Since her mother had died four years earlier, when Chastity was only fifteen, Chastity had to assume the role of hostess at any and all the O’Doyle family’s social events. She had no complaints, infact she had grown to enjoy them. These events were necessary to secure her father’s influence with the men who made all the decisions about everything. She and her father were not a wealthy pair, but he pulled in a sum in the low six figures; she had never wanted for anything. They were honestly content with their lives as it were. Her hourglass figure and flaming red hair caused many to regard her as a great beauty, but it meant nothing to her. All that panting, flapping around and messy exchange of fluids held no interest for her. The hordes of men, who had always flitted around her like bees to a blossom, were a minor irritation. Her father had always kept tight reign on her; bent on keeping her sexual condition the same as her name.

She had not exactly remained true to her name, but her involvements with the opposite sex had been few and unsatisfying: boys her own age were frightfully immature and silly, awed by her mere presence, while the men in her own sphere, (in September she would be entering graduate school) her father claimed, were too old for her. She had the social graces to keep things rolling, to assist her father in maintaining his position among men of true wealth and power, but she saw little value in hurried thrustings and fevered thrashings. She had learned to take charge herself of whatever urges manifested themselves. Her status as an academic had relegated her to a lofty position no boys her age could breach. In addition, the older men she routinely entertained for her father, saw her and treated her, as a child. She sought after and dreamed of, none of it. Her dream was to become the youngest female CEO of a fortune five-hundred company.

She had long ago given up hope of having any semblance of a normal life. She hated whirling around with a bunch of old coots and smiling her inane ‘flight attendant’ smile at everyone. Well, it wouldn’t be long. Three more months and she would be at Yale business school. She was dancing with George Marshall, an important business associate of her father and wealthy forty-five year old, keeping him at bay, listening to his chatter, and interjecting an encouraging phrase now and then, when she noticed a pair of dark eyes fixed on her from across the room. It was as if they bored through her, saw the soft and tender places deep within. Chastity noticed the young man fixated on her but was not in the mood to satify him with her acknowledgement. So she shook her head to dispel the eerie feeling, and went on about her business.

Later that evening, riding home with her father in the limo, she inquired, “Chas, (She was a modern, liberated woman who addressed her father by his given name, which was actually Chastain, but she found that cumbersome.) Who was that man at the party?”
“Which one, hon?”
“I don’t know, I never saw him before. He was tall, well dressed in a very nice pearl gray silk suit. But, it was his eyes I noticed, black, it looked like they were. It was the oddest thing.”

“Oh, I know who you mean. That was Lance Tollidair. He is the CEO of IntraCon. Enormously wealthy. One of those miracle boys. Billionaire before he was twenty-five. He has kind of a reputation as a lady’s man, but he’s only, er, I’m not sure, early thirties, I think. Took a small machine tool business he inherited from his dad, worth maybe two, three million, made some changes, obtained some acquisitions, bought up some failing companies, somehow turned it all into, I don’t know, some say maybe 10 billion.”
“That figures.”
“What does that mean?”
“I could feel his arrogance from across the room.”
“I hear tell he’s a great guy, nice person in general, very charitable. Don’t think he’s in the market for marriage, though.”

“What are you trying to say? Neither am I, ‘in the market’. I have places to go and worlds to conquer. Maybe some day when I’ve amassed my own fortune, I’ll ask him out,” Chastity laughed aloud. Several days went by without incident. Chastity had almost forgotten about the man she had enquired about and her life went along on its day-to-day shuffle. On Wednesday, there was a knock at her door. She answered to find a messenger, hand delivering a message, the first such message she had ever received. It read like an invitation: Mr. Lance Tollidair requests the pleasure of the company of Ms. Chastity O’Doyle at dinner on Friday June 16th at 7 pm – RSVP.

Chastity was stunned. The messenger waited. If she responded in the affirmative, would it be a date? She supposed it would. Her first date in a long time. She blushed strongly, her crimson cheeks augmenting the startling color of her long tresses. “Just a moment please,” she said to the messenger. From her desk, she penned a quick reply on her own custom linen stationary. ‘Ms. Chastity O’Doyle regrets she cannot accept the invitation of Mr.’ . . . she had to look at the message to find it, ‘Lance Tollidair,’ stuffing the letter in a matching envelope and scratching his name on the outside. She returned to the foyer and handed over the letter, tipping the messenger with a five for his trouble. “That should dismiss, Mr. Big Shot arrogant billionaire,” she thought to herself.

On Thursday, she answered the door to find a delivery boy with three dozen American Beauty Roses and a note from Mr. Tollidair: “I am sorry if I have in some way offended you. Won’t you please have dinner with me? Call me.” His phone number was scrawled below. There it was again, ‘Call me’, as if she had nothing better to do with her time. She knew what he had planned for her, didn’t they all!

Chastity put the roses in a cut crystal vase and tossed the note in the trash. She buried her face in the flowers, absorbing their calming aroma. “Well, flowers are always nice, no matter who sends them,” she said to herself. Chastity soon learned that Lance was a very persisted man.
On Monday, FedEx delivered a five-pound box of Belgian chocolates, apparently directly from Belgium. There was no note attached.
On Wednesday, she received notice that a star had been named after her in the official registry.
On Friday, she received a telegram notifying her that a donation of $10,000 had been made in her name to the SPCA. This time there was a note that said simply: “Please call me, 987-3210.”
She had to admit, if nothing else, he was determined. Or was it stubborn? This time she crumbled up the note and shoved it in her pocket.

Late that night, as Chastity was preparing for bed, the balled up note fell from her pocket. She smoothed it out and set it on her nightstand. The next day at noon, as she was on her way to the country club for a round of doubles tennis with friends, she pulled out her keys to start her Jetta and the note fell into her lap. “Hmm, funny,” she thought, but then realized she must have swept the note up from the nightstand with her keys. “It is starting to look as if fate is telling me to call him,” she thought. “What harm could it do? Looks like it’s me that’s being stubborn. What the heck. I have to eat anyway.” She reminded herself to call him after tennis, but of course, she forgot. She spent a delightful afternoon at the club and drove home feeling quite satisfied from the friendship and physical exercise. Her phone rang, while she was driving home about 3:45pm. She answered immediately instead of letting it go to voice mail, and without checking caller ID. For some reason a number flashed in her head, 987-3210. “Hello?” She said.
“Finally, I get to speak to you. Please don’t hang up.” The voice was a deep warm masculine baritone. She paused, way too long.
“Hello,” he said, “Are you there?”
“Yes, I’m here,” Chastity finally answered. “What do you want?”

“What I have wanted since I first laid eyes on you, to ask you out, take you to dinner. However, if there is something else you would like to do, somewhere else, you’d like to go, that’s okay, too. I can eat anytime.”
“When?” she finally replied, sighing deeply, as if surrendering to a force greater than herself.
“YOU WILL! Sorry for shouting. How about tonight? Around eight?”
“Well, okay, yes, yes I will”
“Great, I will pick you up at eight.”
“I live at. . .”
“Oh, I know where you live. I know everything about you.”
Chastity found herself blushing, even through the phone. “What shall I wear?”

This time it was his turn to pause a long time. “Wear whatever you like. Whatever you would wear if you wanted to impress a man. You can wear nothing if you wish. No one would dare question you anyway.”
“Well, thank you, I think, er, Mr., er,”
“Lance, it’s Lance, Chastity.” Thinking he had better hang up while he was ahead, he said, “okay, great, see you at eight then. Bye.”
“Uh, okay, er, bye.”

“Geez,” she thought to herself, “you really came across as a dodo that time, girl. Oh well, no matter, it’s only dinner, just this one time, that’s all.” When she was almost home, a strange picture flashed through her brain. She was sitting at a table in a fancy restaurant; naked except for a striped man’s tie, across from her sat an impeccably dressed Lance Tolladair. She shook off the image and began her list. “I should probably wear my basic black dress, heels, but not too high, evening purse. Hmm, maybe the single strand pearls. Geez, do I have time to do my hair?” she asked herself, looking at the dash clock. It was 4:45. “Just barely, if I hurry.” She paused only a moment to ask herself, “if I care nothing about men, nothing about this arrogant. . . about this, this, Lance person, this date, (she had to admit it was a date), why was she so worried about her damned hair?”

title: Science Fiction
description: On a world of iron storms, even twelve tons of armor might not be enough.
paragraphs: A thick fog lingered over the alien jungle as the sandstorms raged on wildly. Oasis was a giant marble of life with the harshest climate any human had ever encountered yet. Mark could barely see a meter in front of him through the vines that sprawled from the large oak like trees about him and the sand being blown in his face from god knows where. The ecosystem of this new Frontier marvelled him. For a planet that consisted heavily of dense forests and vast bodies of murky water, there was no rationality to the hour long sandstorms that blew through the plains every half hour of the day. The storms were practically the only thing consisted on the red planet.

There was iron in the air, rather, particles of it. This was what gave the planet its red hue and also what caused the storms so frequently. Though the planet had oxygen, the levels of it were so low it could cause most people to suffocate slowly, or quicker if they were in a storm. The red sand slamming into the helm of Mark’s H.A.E.M— Heavy Armoured Exploration Mech— made him all the more glad that he weren’t out in the storm on his own two legs. The dull droning sensation he got from the storm pushing back against him as he marched forward would have paled to the dreadful feeling of small pebbles ripping through his armour if he dare to confront a storm in his Exo-suit.

The H.A.E.M was one of several Mechs from Mark’s base designed to house his consciousness while he explored the wilderness beyond the confines of his electric fences. It was the most appropriate way for him to gather data on his terraformer’s effects on the area beyond the base and the device’s immediate range. The howling of violent winds was punctuated by the churning of gears and whirling of engines as he planted each foot in front of the other, heading north from where his journey had commenced. Mark would have gritted his teeth if he had any to do so, the Mech may have been humanoid to an extent but it did not have need for such. It would have been irrelevant to its build.  The H.A.E.M was a bulky 4 meter tall giant of a machine with spacious compartments on its back for heavy drills, personalized turrets and ammo. It was able to heave materials ten tons its size through rough terrain with easier. It was more suitable for performing maintenance and surveys on and within the terraformer, because of its sturdy build but that was also what made it most suitable for braving the sand storm. From how strenuous it felt forcing his way through the storm, Mark feared that if he had taken any of the other more combat inclined Mechs, then he would have most likely been torn apart by the storm.

‘Everest… Come in- Everest, do you read me?’  He commed time and time again to no avail. The signal was waning, he could barely tell left from right anymore. He couldn’t reach Everest for coordinates over the storm. He still had a mental image of the map Everest had showed him before he set out in the first place and the signal from his stolen cargo didn’t feel too far off. Mark was on his own. “Fuck this…” Mark’s voice grunted from the machine as he started into a heavy sprint. He didn’t like the growing sense of foreboding he got from Everest’s radio silence and he was not going to allow a few pests be the wiser of him.

The Mechs four clawed feet tore through logs in his path and crushed small boulders like they were paper Mache, despite its size the H.A.E.M was quite agile. Mark was like a twelve ton bullet train ripping its path through a forest blindly. Anyone else would have felt invincible riding a Mech that big, Mark wasn’t anyone— especially not after what he had seen the Lurkers do to Mechs like his.

Oasis was just one of hundreds of planets that humanity had decided to make into their home. The climate was one that their domes could within and could easily be handled with a large scale terraformer. The planet’s water was consumable and its forests were overflowing with wildlife, some of which were a little too wild. Before humans, there were the lurkers— a large feral race of scaly humanoids that thrived on the planet. If it hadn’t been for the Mechs and guns at humanity’s disposal, then humans would have never stood a chance against the hostile alien race. Lurkers’ physiology baffled human biologists. Though they seemed humanoid it was merely in appearance and the fact that they were capable of walking on their hind legs with ease. They all possessed five limbs; two clawed feet, two arms and a third clawed limb that grew from right beneath their torso. Their skin was exceptional hard, like that of a hardened rhino. Their eyes were like slits on either side of their long snouted heads and their ears were pointed and hung back behind their skulls.

They were advanced predators that showed frightening intellect and grew to an average of 6ft to 7ft with the muscle equivalent of 6 grown men. They could easily rip through the helm of a Mech or plunge their large third limp, which served as a sort of defense mechanism to their race, through an explorer’s exo-suit to kill them. Mark had seen trained soldiers be overwhelmed by the Lurkers once before, and yet here his was, hunting a pack of them through a storm that left his large singular lens of an eye partially blind. Mark had almost lost his sense of time. The strain was getting to him and he had half the mind to abandon the mission or rather stall it until after the storm had subsided, but no, the consequences of failure were too dire for him to imagine.

title: Drama
description: Four sisters, a house in need of repair, and the fragile promise of a new beginning.
paragraphs: It was a cold summer evening. Beatrice could barely get her eyes to shut. The excitement was driving her crazy, that and the fact that she really had to go. She was just too much of a scaredy-cat to lift herself out of bed to go to the restroom. She crossed her legs anxiously as she glanced about the room. She could barely make out any of the other kids in the dark. But she could tell from their snores that unlike herself, the rest of them were all so sound asleep.
The place was awfully dull and gloomy most of the time, though Orphanages weren’t made for fun. Saint Jane’s Orphanage, had housed Beatrice and her sisters for the past 3 months— since the tragedy.

Beatrice didn’t want to think about it. Sad thoughts made her want to cry, and wanting to cry made it difficult to hold the floodgates of her bladder. Pouting she managed to sit up in her bed as she glanced in the hall’s general direction. Beatrice wasn’t a baby, she could go to the bathroom on her own… but tonight was one of those moonless lights and that only made the large already eerie halls of Saint Jane, twice as scary. It was a moonless evening, the kind of nights that creature liked to go bump in the dark in.  Someone rolling in their bed made a creaking noise that nearly had poor Beatrice jumping at shadows. She glanced to the bed beside hers, she didn’t want to, but now she felt she didn’t have a choice.
“Caro…” She called as quietly as she could manage. “Caro! Caroline! — you still up?”

Caroline, the eldest of her sisters, was staying in a vacant bed beside hers. It was tricky getting someone’s attention while also trying to be as quiet as a mouse. Caroline was spending the night over since they’d all be moving to their new place early the following morning. To Beatrice’s dismay, Caroline didn’t respond. If Caroline was awake then she could have troubled her to at least follow her to the little ladies room, but that wasn’t the case, and Beatrice was almost at her limit. For a moment she thought of trying her luck with waking either Anabelle or Viviane, her other sisters. But as she sat up in bed she realised that wasn’t the brightest idea. Not only were their beds too far from hers, there was no way she could stir them without waking half the room.

Beatrice never was fond of the dark. Sure she wasn’t afraid of the darkness itself, she’d outgrown that fear, but just when she thought she was over her fear of the dark entirely, she just had to join the other kids to stay up telling ghost stories. Now she wasn’t frightened by the dark per say, she was terrified of all the monsters that could be lurking about in it.

Her thoughts and fears then came to a halt as a more pressing need rushed to her mind. Her bladder could not hold it much longer, it felt like it was going to burst at any second. Beatrice weighed her fear against her pride, it was bad enough that a lot of the kids already called her a cry baby, if she wet her bed on her last day there, she could imagine what names they’d come up with. ‘Oh no... that’d be unbearable’ she thought fleetingly as she sat up in her bed.

She crossed her legs to hold it in, which made for climbing out of bed really awkward. She was like a fawn, learning to standing on its legs for the first time in its life. It would have been comical if anyone could see her now, so a part of her felt a tinge of relief that they were all sound asleep.

Beatrice took a deep breath, recounting the juice she’d had and how she’d insisted she didn’t need to go to the bathroom after a couple hours ago, now had her scowling in the dark. ‘Me and my big mouth.’ She berated herself internally as she slowly navigated for the door. A creaking noise announced that her toe had met with the corner of one of the bed frames as Beatrice muffled a yelp with her hands, crumbling to her knees as she did. Once again she was torn between the urge to cry and the urge to pee, neither would have done her any favour.  She forced her bladder to hold it in, or else everyone would wake up to a golden puddle in the middle of the room, and that would have been much more embarrassing than if she wet her bed.

This was by far the hardest she ever had to struggle for anything. Laying on the floor she grew annoyed by her predicament. ‘I wouldn’t have to be battling to get to the bathroom I’d I was home,’ she thought begrudgingly, but then reality set in. She wouldn’t be here if her parents were still alive either. Beatrice took a deep breath, just as her heart felt heavy, a glint under one of the beds caught her attention. ‘Huh...’ She mused as the little glint grew into a ball of light. Beatrice’s eyes widened in amusement as she saw the light slowly hover across the room, then linger at the entrance.

The light wasn’t too bright, not bright enough to bother the others sound asleep, but it was illuminating enough for her to see her way through the room without stubbing her toe again. Curiosity took hold of Beatrice. She managed to get back on her feet without wetting herself, but her laps felt wet with sweat— or at least she hoped it was sweat. She hurried towards the light just as she watched it fade into the hallway. At first she worried that it had gone out, but that wasn’t the case. It had only continued down the hallway.

From where she stood, she realized the light wasn’t some flashlight. Instead, it looked like a sphere, yet scurried about the floor like some sort of animal. Whatever it was, it was illuminating her path, and that was just what she needed. So she followed it through the hall. By this point, she was both too pressed and curious to care about the little details, like what was guiding her through the hall. Passing each door quietly on her way, she finally reached the restroom to the sensation of calm and relief washing over her. Now that she could finally make out the rest of the way, she darted into the bathroom, practically running until she was comfortably sitting in one of the stalls.  It felt like a weight was being lifted off her shoulders as she let her flood gates do their thing.

A sigh of relief escaped her, she was more than grateful for the light that’d led her there. She could see its light behind the door, almost like it’d read her mind. Just as mysteriously as it appeared the light began to fade away, leaving poor Beatrice alone in the dark. All just before she could comfortable.

“Hey… don’t go.” She muttered through a scowl. She was relieved now, but it was short-lived as fear slowly took her. It was awfully quiet, so quiet that Beatrice could hear her heart drumming in her chest. She took deep long breathes and thought, ‘on the Brightside, at least I won’t wet myself.’ But with the look of things, she was almost definitely going to fall asleep on the toilet. It was either that, or she’d need another miracle to get her back to the comfort of her bed.

Beatrice took a deep breath. She knew she had to go back to bed eventually, it was childish just sitting in the stall like that. Reluctantly, she got off the toilet seat, “I’m just going to walk out there, wash my hands, and go back to bed.” She told herself as the resolve to actually follow through with it hadn’t come yet. Squeezing her eyes shut she steeled herself, walking in the dark felt almost as hard as any task she’d lost sleep over.
“Bee? You there?” Caroline’s familiar voice called softly as the light from her torch flooded into the bathroom.

“Caro!” Beatrice chimed back a little too excitedly as she heard Caroline’s footsteps fast approaching, and with light too. For a moment she’d thought it was the light from before, but she was still glad to see her sister instead. She stepped out of the stall to find her sister in the entrance, the torch got in her face a little, but she could still make out Caroline’s tall slender silhouette before she could see her tired face stare quizzically back at her.
“So that’s where you were?” Caroline yawned. “I thought I heard your voice, but when I actually got up to check... you weren’t in your bed.”
“Oh... I just needed to use the bathroom really quick.”

“Without the flashlight?” Caroline mused, “I mean, I left it by your bed for that reason didn’t I? Weren’t you the one that kept whimpering over your fear of the dark? How’d you even get here? Did you walk in the dark? —”
